title: Nexus Retail - POC scoping: latency & throughput SLOs
summary: Discovery/POC scoping focused on defining latency and throughput SLOs for search assistant use case. Discussed TTFT vs TPOT, p95/p99 targets, representative workload, benchmarking plan (synthetic + replay), and pilot timelines. Agreed next steps: Redwood to share benchmark template and security docs; Nexus to provide sample prompt set and traffic profile; schedule benchmark run and follow-up demo week of 11/23.
next_steps: Jordan to send benchmark template and sample JMeter script by 2026-11-10
Maya to upload 1 week of anonymized traffic + sample prompts by 2026-11-13
Priya to schedule 2h benchmark run with Nexus infra week of 2026-11-23
Jordan to share security and SOC2 docs link by 2026-11-10

Maya - Provide anonymized traffic and representative prompts (due 2026-11-13)

transcript:
Header: 2026-11-09 15:00 UTC | Duration: ~60m | Attendees: Jordan (Redwood AE), Priya (Redwood SE), Sam (CSM), Liam (CTO), Maya (ML Eng), Carlos (Infra), Hannah (Product)

Summary (auto): quick recap - define latency SLOs p95/p99, figure out measurement plan, agree data & timeline

00:00 Jordan (AE): hey everyone, thanks for joining, i think we have about an hour, i'll let priya kick off with the technical framing then we can go into your workloads and success criteria
00:18 Priya (SE): yeah thanks jordan, hi liam hi maya, quick context - redwood's typical poc flow is we run a small benchmark using either hosted or dedicated infra, measure TTFT and TPOT across representative prompts, then we do a replay test with your traffic; today i'd like to lock on definitions and targets so we can scope infra and timebox the POC
00:45 Liam (CTO): sounds good, our use case is a search-assistant inside our retail app, mostly short queries and follow-ups so TTFT is really important, but we also care about stable per-token throughput for longer generation when we expand to multi-sentence summaries
01:12 Maya (ML): yeah typical prompt lengths are 20-50 tokens for queries, occasionally up to 250 for summarization, we average about 12 requests/s during peak per region, global footprint - us/eu apac planned later
01:36 Priya (SE): ok that's helpful, so two SLO axes: TTFT (time to first token) and TPOT (time per token after first) — we measure both at p95 and p99. For scoping, we want concrete targets, e.g. p95 TTFT <= 250ms for short queries, p99 TTFT <= 600ms, and p95 TPOT <= 40ms/token, p99 TPOT <= 80ms/token for your short workload. Those are initial proposals, we can tune with benchmark data
02:05 Carlos (Infra): quick q: are those numbers assuming dedicated GPUs or hosted multi-tenant? we are leaning to dedicated for the pilot because of predictability and data isolation
02:25 Priya (SE): good question - the numbers I just gave are achievable on dedicated T4/v100-like pools with optimized batching and kv-cache. On hosted shared infra we typically see more tail variance, so p99 can blow out. If you do dedicated, we can give SLA-like guarantees during the POC window. we'll also test quantized variants of the model which reduce TPOT but may add slight TTFT overhead on cold starts
03:00 Hannah (Product): can you clarify cold start impacts? our app has sporadic traffic outside peak, so cold starts will affect p99 probably
03:18 Priya (SE): yes cold starts can increase TTFT a lot. We define cold as the first request after a scale-to-zero or after a model swap. Our measurement plan: 1) steady-state benchmarks with warm KV cache, 2) cold-start tests (scale from 0), and 3) replay of your real traffic which captures burst patterns. We'll capture both warm p95/p99 and cold p95/p99. For scale-to-zero we expect TTFT to increase to multiple seconds unless you provision warm pools
04:05 Maya (ML): on measurement, do you measure TTFT from client send or from arrival at the load balancer? we need to line up metrics with our observability so we can compare
04:22 Priya (SE): we typically measure at the Redwood ingress (time request received by platform) to first token emitted. But for the POC we can also instrument from your client if you prefer. We'll provide a tracer span map and a prometheus-compatible metric for TTFT and TPOT so you can compare with your telemetry
05:00 Liam (CTO): ok good. about success criteria: we need p95 TTFT < 300ms and p99 TPOT < 90ms for the initial pilot, otherwise we can't proceed to integration. Does that sound reasonable to you?
05:20 Jordan (AE): that's a clear sweet spot. i'd note we might push for slightly tighter on p95 TTFT once we tune batching and caching but we should capture baseline first
05:39 Priya (SE): yes and small caveat: TTFT is highly sensitive to prompt size, model choice, and whether you call function/tooling or streaming. For example, if you use function-calls or want structured output that increases initial latency due to decoding. We'll capture breakdown: tokenizer time, model kernel time, network transfer, and marshalling overhead
06:10 Carlos (Infra): about workload sizing: maya said 12 req/s peak per region, do you have 95th pct distribution across endpoints? e.g., 80% short queries, 15% medium, 5% long?
06:30 Maya (ML): yes approx: 78% short (<50 tokens), 17% medium (50-150), 5% long (150-400). token generation distribution also skewed right for summarization flows
07:00 Priya (SE): perfect, we'll use that distribution in the synthetic generator. For tokenization we need average tokens in and tokens out per request, please add that to the data drop. Also we need to know concurrency per connection - are requests bursty or smoothed?
07:18 Maya (ML): bursty, we have flash sale periods where concurrency spikes 4x for short windows, average burst 48 req/s across cluster for 60-120s
07:36 Priya (SE): then we will run a burst test: baseline sustained traffic at your avg peak (12 rps), then 4x spike for 2 minutes, then observe p95/p99 behavior and any queuing. We'll capture queuing delay separately from model processing time
08:05 Liam (CTO): what's your approach to batching? we worry about batching increasing latency for short queries
08:22 Priya (SE): batching is a knob - continuous batching with latency budgets. Our runtime can target e.g. maximum latency budget per request and batch while staying under that. For your short queries we would likely set a small batch window (<10ms) and smaller batch sizes to keep TTFT low while still getting some throughput benefit. We'll show tradeoff curves in the benchmark results
08:58 Jordan (AE): also pricing and cost tradeoffs come in - locking dedicated nodes ups cost but reduces tail. We'll include expected token cost projection for both dedicated and hosted during the POC deliverable
09:20 Carlos (Infra): security note - we need to validate KMS integration and audit logs, we want to see audit-trail for every request during POC
09:34 Jordan (AE): yes we'll share the SOC2 docs and the audit-log integration guide. Priya, can you include log schema in the deliverable?
09:42 Priya (SE): yep will include event schema and span IDs, plus prometheus and opentelemetry mappings.
10:05 Hannah (Product): timeline - what's realistic to finish initial benchmark and have a go/no-go?
10:20 Jordan (AE): if we get your traffic and short-lived creds by 11/13, we can run baseline tests week of 11/23 and have results + recommendations by 11/27. So decision point before end of November
10:40 Maya (ML): ok that's fine, we'll try to get the data by friday 11/13
10:50 Priya (SE): measurement plan recap: 1) synthetic steady-state warm cache runs with representative prompt distribution capturing p50/p95/p99 TTFT and TPOT; 2) cold-start experiments (scale from zero and model swap) capturing cold p95/p99; 3) replay test with your anonymized traffic to capture burst behavior and queuing; 4) stress test for saturation to find max sustainable RPS for each target latency bucket; 5) capture kernel-level breakdown and export span maps and prometheus metrics. We'll provide a JMeter/grpc-bench script and a template for the sample prompts and anonymized payloads
12:05 Liam (CTO): stated success criteria in plain terms: 'pilot considered success if warm p95 TTFT <= 300ms and warm p95 TPOT <= 50ms during your typical peak; plus cold p99 TTFT < 2s if dedicated pools are pre-warmed; and no data residency/security blockers'
12:30 Jordan (AE): good, we'll translate to the POC acceptance doc and include the exact metric names and dashboards to monitor. any objections?
12:45 Carlos (Infra): just one more - do you require inbound NAT or can we give out egress to your test harness? we prefer inbound for better network parity
13:00 Priya (SE): inbound is fine, we'll use short-lived credentials and a controlled test endpoint. We'll also provide an option to run Redwood's benchmark inside your VPC if you prefer full parity (we have a VPC-side runner that we've used with other customers)
13:28 Maya (ML): perfect, also include model variant guidance - we want to try a 7b and a 13b open model initially, do you support quantized 4-bit for 13b?
13:45 Priya (SE): yes we support q4 and q8 for certain families. We'll list compatible quantization profiles and expected TPOT improvements vs slight quality tradeoffs. We'll include that matrix in the deliverable
14:10 Hannah (Product): ok can you also include recommended rollout plan - canary percentages and automatic fallback to a cheaper model if latency spikes?
14:28 Priya (SE): yes our rollout options support canary and A/B with automatic fallback policies; we'll include recommended policies in the POC playbook
14:50 Jordan (AE): great, let's recap next steps: jordan send template and security docs, maya upload traffic and prompts, carlos provide creds/firewall info, priya schedule runs. We'll aim for a benchmark week of 11/23 and results 11/27.
15:10 Liam (CTO): thanks everyone, appreciate the clarity. we'll follow up in email with data share link.
15:20 Jordan (AE): thanks all, end of call

Notes: transcript contains some ASR errors; speaker tags sometimes generic. References: Redwood docs link (shared): https://redwood.internal/docs/poc-benchmark-template (redacted), security pack: https://redwood.internal/sec/soc2.pdf (redacted)
